entries.title: Ciira v Republic (Criminal Appeal E123 of 2023)
entries.principle: The prosecution must prove robbery with violence beyond reasonable doubt; the court will examine the identification evidence and the chain of custody.

entries.title: Kabacho & Another v Republic (Criminal Appeal 59 of 2019)
entries.principle: A conviction for robbery with violence must be supported by credible evidence; the court will re-evaluate the evidence and may reduce the sentence where appropriate.

entries.title: Republic v SO (Sexual Offence E020 of 2025)
entries.principle: Sexual offences require proof of the act and the absence of consent; the court must evaluate the credibility of the complainant and the accused.

entries.title: Katiba Institute v Attorney General & Others (Robbery with Violence)
entries.principle: The offence of robbery with violence must be defined with sufficient precision; arbitrary or disproportionate sentencing engages constitutional rights.

entries.title: Republic v Loriu (Murder Case 32 of 2017)
entries.principle: The prosecution must prove the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt; the court weighs the evidence as a whole, including circumstantial evidence.

entries.title: Republic v Kalii (Murder Case 7 of 2017)
entries.principle: A murder charge requires proof of malice aforethought; the prosecution must establish the actus reus and mens rea beyond reasonable doubt.

entries.title: Francis Karioko Muruatetu & Another v Republic
entries.principle: The mandatory death penalty is unconstitutional as it deprives the court of the discretion to consider the circumstances of the offender and the offence, violating the right to a fair trial and human dignity.
entries.facts: Francis Karioko Muruatetu and another were convicted of murder and sentenced to the mandatory death penalty. They challenged the constitutionality of the mandatory death penalty. The case raised questions of sentencing discretion and human dignity.
entries.holding: The Supreme Court held that the mandatory death penalty is unconstitutional as it deprives the court of discretion to consider the circumstances of the offender and the offence. The Court directed that sentencing guidelines be developed for murder cases.
entries.judges: Maraga CJ, Mwilu DCJ, Ibrahim, Ojwang, Wanjala and Ndung'u SCJJ (Supreme Court)

entries.title: Republic v JM (Sexual Offence 20 of 2016)
entries.principle: The Sexual Offences Act creates specific offences with defined elements; the prosecution must prove each element, and the court must safeguard the rights of the accused and the complainant.
